phases.subheadline: Comfort, energy, and care matched to your period days

pages.title: Your body on your period
pages.body:
The uterine lining is shedding. Prostaglandins can trigger cramps, lower-back ache, loose stools, and a heavier sense of fatigue — especially on days 1–3 when flow is often strongest.

Your body is doing real work. Mild discomfort is common; pain that stops you from standing, soaking through protection hourly, or dizziness deserves a clinician’s attention.
pages.detail_body: A warm compress on the lower abdomen, slow walking, and magnesium-rich foods. Intense workouts can wait until energy returns.

pages.title: Ease, don’t force
pages.body: Hormone levels (estrogen and progesterone) are at their lowest. That can flatten motivation and make cold feel colder. Soften your to-do list and protect sleep tonight.

pages.title: Body comfort toolkit
pages.body: Choose 1–2 that feel realistic today.

tips.title: Heat therapy
tips.body: A heating pad or warm shower for 15–20 minutes often eases uterine cramps better than pushing through.

tips.title: Iron awareness
tips.body: If flow is moderate to heavy, include iron-friendly foods (lentils, leafy greens, lean meat) with vitamin C.

tips.title: Hydration cue
tips.body: Dehydration can worsen headaches and cramps — aim for steady sips, not one big gulp.

tips.title: Bathroom breaks
tips.body: Prostaglandins can speed digestion; keep tissues and comfort items handy.

tips.title: Position change
tips.body: Knees-to-chest or a gentle child’s pose can relieve lower-back pressure for some.

pages.title: Know your red flags
pages.body: Soaking a pad/tampon every hour for several hours, clots larger than a coin, fainting, or pain that doesn’t respond to usual care — contact a clinician. These tips are educational only.

pages.title: An inward day is valid
pages.body: Many people feel quieter, more sensitive, or less social early in their period. That isn’t laziness — it’s a hormonal low. Matching your pace to your energy usually works better than fighting it.

pages.title: Mood & energy supports
pages.body: Small buffers protect your bandwidth.

tips.title: Shorter plans
tips.body: Swap a long outing for something closer and shorter if you can.

tips.title: Light exposure
tips.body: Morning daylight for 5–10 minutes can gently lift mood without a hard workout.

tips.title: Warm layers
tips.body: Temperature swings are common — dress so you can add or remove a layer.

tips.title: Name the feeling
tips.body: A quick note in your log (“tired + crampy”) helps you spot patterns next cycle.

tips.title: Ask for help
tips.body: If you share a household, one delegated chore today is a fair ask.

pages.title: Why energy dips
pages.body: With estrogen low and blood loss underway, oxygen delivery and mood neurotransmitters can feel off. Sleep quality may also drop if pain interrupts the night.
pages.detail_body: An earlier wind-down, dimmer screens, and a warm drink often beat scrolling past midnight.

pages.title: You are enough today
pages.body: Resting is productive when your body is shedding. Tomorrow’s energy may already feel different.

pages.title: Nourish through your flow
pages.body: Steady fuel beats perfection.

tips.title: Iron + C plate
tips.body: Beans, greens, or lean meat with citrus, peppers, or tomatoes.

tips.title: Steady snacks
tips.body: Banana with nut butter, yogurt, or cheese and crackers blunt crashes.

tips.title: Warm meals
tips.body: Soups and cooked veggies often sit better than cold salads during cramps.

tips.title: Salt awareness
tips.body: If you’re bloated, ease up on ultra-salty packaged snacks.

tips.title: Comfort without guilt
tips.body: A small treat alongside protein is fine — restriction often backfires.

pages.title: Care that fits real life
pages.body: Period care is more than products. It’s how you move, eat, rest, and speak to yourself. Build a tiny kit: heat, hydration, preferred protection, and one comfort snack.
pages.detail_body: Change protection regularly and use what feels secure — pads, cups, discs, or period underwear.

pages.title: Movement that helps
pages.body: Gentle beats intense on heavy days.

tips.title: 5–15 min walk
tips.body: Light walking can ease cramps for many without draining you.

tips.title: Hip stretch
tips.body: Cat-cow or a supported squat hold for 30–60 seconds.

tips.title: Skip the PR
tips.body: Save hard intervals and heavy PRs for follicular or ovulation energy.

tips.title: Rest day is allowed
tips.body: If flow is heavy or sleep was poor, full rest is smart training.

pages.title: Listen, then adjust
pages.body: Your cycle is data. What helped last period? Keep that. What didn’t? Drop it without judgment.

pages.title: Signals many people notice

tips.body: Usually strongest early; heat + rest often help.

tips.title: Fatigue
tips.body: Extra sleep and iron-friendly meals can support recovery.

tips.title: Headache

tips.title: Backache

tips.title: Mood dips

pages.title: Trust your instincts
pages.body: If symptoms are new, suddenly worse, or worry you, a clinician visit is appropriate. Apps educate — they don’t diagnose.

pages.body: A little setup makes day 2 kinder.

tips.title: Charge your heat pad
tips.body: Or set out a hot-water bottle tonight.

tips.title: Lay out clothes
tips.body: Comfortable waistbands reduce morning friction.

tips.body: Block 15 minutes of white space if your day is packed.

pages.title: After your period — the rebuild
pages.body:
Estrogen is climbing as follicles mature in the ovaries. Many people notice clearer thinking, brighter mood, better skin, and more motivation for workouts or creative projects.

Think of this as your cycle’s spring: recovery from the bleed and rising capacity.
pages.detail_body: Rising estrogen supports serotonin pathways for many — which is why mood and energy often lift together.

pages.title: Build momentum
pages.body: This is a strong window for new habits, strength training, skill practice, and projects that need focus — if you feel up for them.

pages.title: Body signals to notice
pages.body: Optional cues — not everyone feels all of them.

tips.title: Strength session

tips.title: Social plans

tips.title: Creative sprints

pages.title: Mood on the rise
pages.body: As estrogen increases, many people feel more optimistic and outgoing. That doesn’t mean you must be “on” all day — it means you have more capacity to spend where it matters.
pages.detail_body: Pick one meaningful task and one restorative break. Balance keeps the lift sustainable.

pages.title: Fresh-start energy
pages.body: You’re past the heaviest bleed days. Celebrate small wins without stacking your calendar edge-to-edge.

pages.body: As energy returns, pair movement with real meals. Skipping food to “feel lighter” often backfires with fatigue and irritability.

pages.body: Consistency beats a perfect day. One solid meal and one intentional movement already count.

pages.title: Around ovulation
pages.body:
An egg may be released from an ovary. Estrogen peaks then dips; luteinizing hormone (LH) surges beforehand. Cervical mucus often becomes clearer and more stretchy. Libido and social energy can feel higher.

This window is short. Prediction apps estimate — they don’t confirm ovulation for every cycle.
pages.detail_body: Fertile-window estimates are not birth control. Use contraception if you are avoiding pregnancy.

pages.title: Stay aware, stay kind
pages.body: Mild one-sided twinges (mittelschmerz) can happen. Sharp, severe, or one-sided pain with vomiting or fainting needs urgent care.

pages.title: Body cues some people notice

pages.title: Channel the peak

pages.detail_body: Desire is not obligation. Your boundaries matter on high-energy days too.

pages.title: After ovulation — the luteal stretch
pages.body:
Progesterone rises to support a potential pregnancy. If there’s no pregnancy, both progesterone and estrogen fall before your period — and that drop is strongly linked with PMS for many.

Bloating, breast tenderness, warmer body temperature, earlier hunger, and shorter patience are common. You’re not imagining it.
pages.detail_body: The week before your period is when mood and comfort shifts often peak. Tracking helps you plan buffer days.

pages.title: Soften the edges
pages.body: You don’t need to match follicular intensity. Strength plus recovery often feels better than max HIIT when progesterone is high.

pages.title: Body changes many notice
pages.body: Normalize the list — then support yourself.

tips.title: Bloat
tips.body: Water retention and slower digestion can make waistbands feel tighter.

tips.title: Tender breasts
tips.body: Supportive bras and reduced caffeine help some people.

tips.title: Hunger up
tips.body: Earlier or larger meals aren’t a failure — fuel intentionally.

tips.title: Warmer sleep
tips.body: You may run warmer; lighter bedding can help.

tips.title: Skin changes
tips.body: Oilier skin or breakouts can appear premenstrually.

pages.title: This phase passes
pages.body: Luteal isn’t forever. Knowing “I’m in luteal” can turn self-blame into a plan: sleep, food, fewer stacked deadlines.

pages.title: Steady the luteal stretch
pages.body: Small buffers make a big difference.

tips.title: Sleep priority
tips.body: Aim for a consistent wind-down — progesterone can disrupt sleep for some.

tips.title: Salt & bloat
tips.body: If puffiness bothers you, ease ultra-salty packaged foods.

tips.title: Mood tools
tips.body: Walks, journaling, or a 2-minute breath break when irritability spikes.

tips.title: Calendar triage
tips.body: Move non-urgent conflict conversations if you can.

tips.title: Social dose
tips.body: Prefer smaller plans over packed nights if you’re tender.

pages.title: Why mood can wobble
pages.body: Falling hormones before your period affect neurotransmitters involved in mood regulation. Stress, poor sleep, and low blood sugar make the wobble louder.
pages.detail_body: Protein-rich meals, daylight, and a fixed bedtime are boring — and effective for many.

pages.title: You are enough
pages.body: Cravings and lower patience are hormonal context — not a character flaw. Plan comfort without guilt.

pages.title: Irritability first-aid
pages.body: Use when you’re already mid-spiral.

tips.title: Pause texting
tips.body: Draft, don’t send, for 10 minutes.

tips.title: Blood sugar check
tips.body: Eat something with protein before hard talks.

tips.title: Temperature change
tips.body: Cool water on wrists or a short outside breath.

tips.title: Name it aloud
tips.body: “I’m in luteal and overloaded” can reduce shame.

tips.title: Ask for space
tips.body: A 20-minute alone reset is allowed.

pages.body: Balance comfort with staying steady.

tips.title: Complex carbs

tips.title: Warm meals

tips.title: Protein at dinner

tips.title: Pair sweets
tips.body: If you want dessert, add yogurt or nuts alongside.

pages.title: Comfort without chaos
pages.body: Restriction + luteal hunger is a rough combo. Build a “yes” list: foods that satisfy and still leave you feeling okay an hour later.
pages.detail_body: Toast with peanut butter, warm oatmeal, or a cheese quesadilla can beat grazing on sweets alone.

tips.title: Brain fog
tips.body: Write things down; reduce multitasking when possible.

pages.title: There’s a higher-support path
pages.body: If premenstrual symptoms are severe, disrupt work/relationships, or include hopelessness, talk to a clinician. PMDD and other conditions are real and treatable — don’t tough it out alone.

pages.body: Needing different food, movement, and social dose across the month is human. Design for your phases — that’s wisdom, not weakness.
